tldr: This paper shows that without relying on motion capture or generative motion priors, a humanoid can traverse an 85 m challenging chained course in a deployment-fidelity simulator with a 90% success rate, by pairing terrain-classifier-routed Mixture-of-Experts with a continuous foothold refinement planner.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of the proposed system and the boundary between training and deployment. At deployment on a physical robot or in the evaluation simulator, only the sensed local elevation map is provided as input; privileged terrain labels are used solely for training the gating classifier and conditioning the critic.
overview:
To enable humanoid robots to traverse uneven terrains like rough ground, stairs, and hurdles, the dominant approach retargets motion capture (MoCap) data, trains a generative model as a motion prior, and distills it into a reinforcement learning policy. However, this pipeline incurs enormous costs for data collection and tuning.

In response, the authors ask a simple question: is this complex MoCap-derived motion generation pipeline truly necessary? Instead, they propose a system combining a five-expert Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) routed by predicting terrain categories from a sensed elevation grid, and a lightweight model-based foothold planner that continuously refines foothold candidates using closed-form cost gradients.

For evaluation, beyond the fast simulator used for training, they built a second "deployment-fidelity" simulator that replicates real-robot setups down to sensor latency and ROS communication stacks. Tested on an approximately 85 m chained course across five distinct terrains (slopes, rough ground, scattered obstacles, stairs, and hurdles), the system crossed the entire course end-to-end 18 out of 20 times (90%).

In ablation studies, an ablated model using a single network instead of the MoE and omitting continuous foothold refinement collapsed to a 0% success rate on both stairs and hurdles. Furthermore, the paper provides in-depth insights into failure modes, such as how label-free routers collapse to uniform activation and why single-terrain training demands different capabilities than chained-terrain traversal.
contributions: Demonstrated a humanoid locomotion system that completes a long-distance rough-terrain course in a deployment-fidelity simulator with a 90% success rate, without using any motion capture data or generative motion priors.

Proposed a continuous foothold refinement planner that replaces discrete grid searches with six steps of closed-form gradient descent on a bilinearly interpolated terrain-cost field, substantially reducing foothold errors.

Showed through systematic component studies that label-free MoE routing collapses toward uniform activation, whereas distilling privileged categorical labels overwhelmingly outperforms self-supervised terrain embeddings.

sections.heading: Can We Ditch MoCap and Generative Motion Priors?
sections.summary: State-of-the-art perceptive humanoid locomotion relies heavily on MoCap and generative models, but this paper presents an alternative path without them. Powered by a terrain-classifier-driven MoE and a continuous refinement planner, the robot traversed an 85 m course on a deployment software stack with a 90% success rate.
sections.details:
Recent perceptive humanoid locomotion research has largely converged on a pipeline: retarget human MoCap data, train a generative motion prior, and distill it into an RL policy. However, the authors argue that this heavy pipeline is not strictly necessary.

The proposed system relies on two core pillars. First, in place of a motion prior, it uses a five-expert MoE policy routed by a terrain classifier. Second, in place of MoCap contact behaviors, it employs a model-based foothold planner that continuously refines rough foothold choices via closed-form gradient descent along a bilinearly interpolated terrain-cost field.

Evaluation was performed in a deployment-fidelity simulator that runs the exact same perception-to-actuation software stack (including ROS communication and perception pipelines) as the physical robot. On an 85 m five-segment chained waypoint course, it achieved an end-to-end traversal rate of 18 out of 20 runs (90%). The paper aims to demonstrate that this system design works and to pinpoint exactly which components account for performance and which do not.

sections.heading: Prior Work and Why Those Methods Failed Here
sections.summary: The paper surveys three related lines of work: terrain-conditioned MoE, self-supervised representations, and model-based foothold planning. In particular, it reimplements and evaluates prior label-free MoE routers to understand why they collapse to uniform expert selection.
sections.details:
Prior work on perceptive humanoid rough-terrain locomotion falls into three broad categories.

The first is terrain-conditioned Mixture-of-Experts (MoE). Prior studies such as CMoE, TAGA, CoRe-MoE, and CTS-MoE train routers without explicit terrain labels using self-supervised contrastive learning (like SwAV-style clustering) to tackle tasks like gap leaping. However, these works often report that naive gating networks easily collapse into picking experts uniformly. When the authors tested CMoE's SwAV/Sinkhorn–Knopp routing on their task, the router similarly failed to differentiate experts and collapsed to uniform selection.

The second is self-supervised state and terrain representation learning. Many works pretrain representations from depth camera feeds using contrastive objectives (such as CPC, TCN, and ATC). In this study, the authors also built a temporal-contrastive encoder trained on the robot's depth stream to benchmark against existing representation learning methods.

The third is model-based foothold planning. Planning footholds under capturability constraints via mixed-integer quadratic programming (MIQP) or the Divergent Component of Motion (DCM) is well studied. The planner here avoids timing optimization and global search, focusing instead on lightweight continuous local gradient refinement that runs directly within GPU-parallel rollouts.

sections.heading: System Architecture: Privileged Label Distillation and Continuous Foothold Refinement
sections.summary: This section covers the perception stack, MoE gating, continuous foothold planner, and critic design. At deployment, privileged inputs are completely absent; the robot predicts terrain categories from an onboard elevation grid and refines foot placements down to sub-grid accuracy along interpolated cost gradients.
sections.details:
As shown in Figure F1, the system architecture maintains a strict boundary: privileged information is used only during training, while deployment relies solely on onboard sensory inputs.

### III-A Exteroception and Two Simulators
The robot observes a local elevation grid $\mathcal{H}_{t}$ of size $1.2\,\mathrm{m} \times 1.0\,\mathrm{m}$ (resolution $5\,\mathrm{cm}$) around itself. The control frequency is $50\,\mathrm{Hz}$. Training uses a fast MuJoCo-based simulator, whereas evaluation runs inside a deployment-fidelity simulator that models perception registration latency and communication overhead.

### III-B Mixture of Experts (MoE) and Gating Classifier
Terrain categories are fixed to five classes ($K=5$): rough, stairs up, stairs down, gap, and hurdle. The gating network $g_\phi$ is trained independently with cross-entropy loss against privileged simulation labels $y_t$ without passing policy gradients. At deployment, it routes the policy either by picking the argmax expert (hard) or by blending via softmax weights (soft). The gating classifier reaches $97.1\%$ accuracy in offline validation.

### III-C Continuous Local Foothold Refinement Planner
Locomotion stability relies on a nominal DCM-based stride target. While traditional discrete planners search over a grid for the lowest-cost cell, this method bilinearly interpolates terrain costs $\mathcal{I}[\cdot]$ (elevation, step height, slope), enabling closed-form cost gradients $\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}\mathcal{J}$ at any continuous position $\mathbf{x}$. By taking $N=6$ gradient descent steps from the nominal target, it finds an optimal placement free from grid-cell boundaries. Foot trajectory guidance uses quadratic Bézier curves.

### III-D Terrain Representation, Critic, and Training
A self-supervised encoder extracts a 64-dimensional latent vector $a_t$ from onboard depth streams via temporal-contrastive learning (InfoNCE) to condition the critic through FiLM modulation. The policy is trained using PPO.

captions.F1: System inputs/outputs and the boundary between training and deployment. Solid lines (blue/green) show modules shared between the simulator and the physical robot stack, while dashed orange lines indicate privileged information available only during training. The privileged label $y_t$ supervises the gating classifier, which then routes the five experts during deployment via predicted gates.

sections.heading: Evaluation Protocol: Forced-Routing and Rigorous Baselines
sections.summary: The authors established a sim-to-sim course evaluation and a forced-routing protocol to confirm whether experts truly specialize. Rigorous metrics account for class imbalance to rule out coincidental performance.
sections.details:
The evaluation protocol was designed with great care.

### Sim-to-Sim Course
Inside the deployment-fidelity simulator, an 84.6 m course concatenates five terrain segments: slopes, rough fields, scattered obstacles, stairs up/down, and hurdles. Each segment is scored both as an isolated standalone test and as part of the continuous chained course, separating run-up and fatigue effects.

### Forced-Routing Protocol
To verify whether the MoE genuinely differentiates functions, trained models were re-evaluated under five routing modes:
- trained: standard predicted routing from the gating classifier
- top-1: hard selection of the single highest-probability expert
- random-hard: uniformly random expert selection at every control step (control group)
- uniform: unrouted equal averaging across all experts
- oracle: forced routing using true privileged simulation labels

If the experts had simply collapsed into an ensemble of similar policies, switching them at random would not drop the reward. Conversely, if experts are truly specialized to specific terrains, the random-hard mode changing experts every step should cause catastrophic failure, exposing the true degree of specialization.

sections.heading: Deployment-Fidelity Sim-to-Sim: 85 m Traversal vs. Ablation Collapse
sections.summary: Configuration B, equipped with privileged-label gating and continuous foothold refinement, crossed the grueling 85 m chained course with a 90% success rate. In contrast, the baseline with a single network and discrete planning dropped to 0% on stairs and hurdles.
sections.details:
Here are the results of testing Configuration B (privileged-label gate + continuous foothold planner) inside the deployment-fidelity simulator.

### Course Completion Rates
When scored on individual segments alone, Configuration B succeeded 20 out of 20 times (100%) on slopes, rough terrain, obstacles, and stairs, and 18/20 (90%) on hurdles. On the chained course spanning all five segments end-to-end, it completed 18 of 20 runs (90%, Wilson 95% CI: 69.9–97.2%). Both failed runs were falls, not timeouts.

### Comparison with Ablations
The system was compared against an ablated baseline combining a single policy network (no MoE) with a discrete grid search planner (no continuous refinement). While it performed comparably on gentle slopes and rough ground, its success dropped to 65% on scattered obstacles, and collapsed to 0 out of 20 runs (0% success) on both stairs and hurdles (Fisher's exact test, $p < 10^{-8}$).

Interestingly, on flat terrain, the ablated model walked roughly 26–30% faster than the proposed system with half the stumble count and energy expenditure. This quantitatively illustrates a trade-off: the proposed system trades off flat-ground walking efficiency to purchase the traversal capability needed to cross extreme terrains that a single network cannot solve.

sections.heading: Component Analysis: What Worked and What Didn't?
sections.summary: Continuous foothold refinement significantly cuts foot placement errors, while label-free routers collapse to uniform expert selection. Furthermore, while a single network suffices when trained on single terrains, an MoE is indispensable for continuous multi-terrain courses.
sections.details:
The contribution of each component was analyzed under a matched training budget (20k iterations).

### VI-A Effect of the Foothold Planner
Comparing the continuous planner (G) against a conventional discrete grid planner (H) showed that continuous refinement significantly reduced foothold errors on stairs down and hurdles. As seen in Figure F3, the continuous planner searches around the nominal foothold target, and optimization moves $72.4\%$ of placements across at least one grid-cell boundary. This provides clear proof of true sub-grid correction beyond the coarse $5\,\mathrm{cm}$ grid cells.

### VI-B The Reality of Routing: Collapse of Label-Free Routers
As shown in Figure F4, the gate trained on privileged labels cleanly differentiates experts along the diagonal by terrain (concentration score $S=0.90$). In contrast, the label-free (self-supervised) router (E) yielded a concentration score of $S=0.21$ (theoretical uniform random is $0.20$), collapsing into an equal distribution across all experts. Adding a Switch Transformer load-balancing loss did not prevent this collapse.

In the forced-routing experiments (Table IV), forcing top-1 routing preserved performance with a $+1.8\%$ reward change, whereas random-hard routing every step caused rewards to plunge by $-61.1\%$. This confirms that individual experts learned clear functional specialization.

### VI-C Insights from Negative Results
- One expert equals five on single-terrain training: When an episode stays within a single terrain type during training, a single network (F) matches or outperforms the MoE. However, it breaks down completely once deployed onto continuous multi-terrain courses.
- Limits of self-supervised embeddings: Latent representations $a_t$ learned from onboard depth streams captured terrain features with $59.9\%$ accuracy (rather than gait phase), but as an input to the critic, they achieved only a $2.6\%$ success rate compared to $15.3\%$ when conditioned on privileged labels, underscoring the decisive superiority of privileged categorical labels.

captions.F3: Behavior of the continuous foothold planner (G). Across (a) stairs down, (b) hurdles, (c) stairs up, and (d) gaps, foot placements are continuously refined from the search box around the nominal stride (cyan rectangle) toward safe footholds (bright markers) via closed-form gradient descent.
captions.F4: Gate mass allocation across terrains at the final checkpoint. The gate trained on privileged labels (left) cleanly specializes experts along the diagonal, whereas the label-free router (right) collapses into near-uniform allocation (around 0.20) on every terrain.

sections.heading: Scope and Limitations: What Remains Unanswered
sections.summary: The authors outline notable limitations: no direct head-to-head comparison with latest motion-prior methods, evaluation restricted to high-fidelity simulation rather than physical hardware, and lack of global optimality or timing optimization in the foothold planner.
sections.details:
The authors transparently discuss the scope and limitations of their study.

- No direct comparison to competing motion-prior methods: Key prior works using MoCap and motion priors do not have open-source codebases, and reimplementing them from text failed to reproduce reported results. To avoid presenting unfair strawman baselines, direct comparisons were omitted. Thus, the authors do not claim superiority over motion priors.
- No physical hardware experiments: Validation was conducted inside a deployment-fidelity simulator that fully emulates the physical robot's software stack; testing on hardware remains future work.
- Seed and training variance: Performance varies across random seeds, and the 90% completion rate comes from a single seed of Configuration B.
- Planner simplifications: Designed primarily for high throughput on GPUs (running in a few milliseconds per step), the foothold planner relies on local gradient descent and does not include simultaneous step-timing optimization, global optimality guarantees, or formal safety guarantees across disconnected regions.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Crossing Rough Terrain Without MoCap
sections.summary: Even without motion priors, combining a privileged-label-routed MoE with a continuous foothold planner achieved a 90% traversal rate in high-fidelity simulation. This system study clearly isolates what works and what does not.
sections.details:
This paper demonstrates that a humanoid robot can cross an 85 m challenging terrain course in a deployment-fidelity simulator with a 90% success rate without motion capture data or pretrained generative motion priors, relying instead on a terrain-classifier-guided Mixture-of-Experts and a continuous foothold refinement planner.

Detailed analyses showed that gating plays a decisive role (randomizing experts reduced rewards by $-61\%$) and that while self-supervised representations encode terrain features to an extent, they fall short of direct distillation from privileged labels for critic conditioning. Along with a deployment-grade simulation environment, this paper presents a practical alternative path for humanoid locomotion control.

takeaways: Advanced rough-terrain humanoid traversal is achievable without MoCap or generative motion priors by pairing a terrain-classifier-routed MoE with a continuous foothold planner.
Label-free MoE routers in RL tend to collapse toward uniform expert activation; explicitly training a classifier with privileged terrain labels resolves this failure mode.

Compared to discrete grid search on coarse elevation maps (5 cm cells), continuous closed-form gradient descent (just 6 steps) on bilinearly interpolated cost fields significantly cuts foot placement errors on steps and stairs.
While a single generalist network performs adequately when trained on isolated terrains, a specialized MoE becomes essential when traversing continuous multi-terrain courses.
limitations: Experiments were conducted in a deployment-fidelity simulator (sim-to-sim) without physical robot hardware validation.
No direct head-to-head comparison against state-of-the-art MoCap-based methods on a shared benchmark.
The foothold planner relies on local gradient descent for GPU speed, lacking step timing co-optimization, global optimality guarantees, or formal safety guarantees.
